label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
**The house in Glenmore**

I have agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore, and it closes on Friday the 15th of January. Some of you know this already. Some of you know it because you heard it from somebody other than me, and that is the first thing I have to put right.

I'm writing it here because this is what Úna set the blog up for all those years ago, so that the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds would get the family's news when the rest of us got it, and not three weeks later at the tail end of somebody else's phone call. I would sooner say this once, in full, to all of you together, than have it go round in bits and come out a little different every time. It is long, and there are hard things in it. Make tea first.

The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November. I had every intention of telling each of you myself before it went any further, and I was too slow about it. Word got out ahead of me, as it will in this family, and a good few of you learned that the old Mulkerrin place was sold from a message on your phone. That was my own fault and nobody else's, and I am sorry for it. I could give you reasons for the delay, but they would only be excuses, and I spent too many years listening to excuses about homework to offer you any of my own.

There is a second thing I got wrong, and it is bigger than the timing. I made up my mind without talking to the people who love that house. The decision was mine to make, and I would make it again, but I could have picked up the phone and said "this is what I'm thinking" before it was done, and I didn't. Some of you would have argued with me. You'd have been entitled to, and I'd have been the better for hearing it.

I'll say now, so there is no confusion further down, that I am sorry for how you found out and I am not sorry for the decision. I have had to keep those two things apart in my own head, and I'd ask you to do the same while you read the rest.

Here is why I did it.

Tom died in March 2024. Ever since, I have driven out to Glenmore every fortnight, forty minutes each way, to air the house and check the pipes. I open the windows, run the taps, walk through every room, close it all up again and drive home. I have done it in every kind of weather, and I have got to know that road better than I ever wanted to. For a long time I told myself I was minding the place for the family. I think now I was going out so that I wouldn't have to decide anything. As long as the windows were being opened, the question could wait another fortnight.

In September I had Ó Flaithearta's out to survey the roof. The slates need doing and so does the back chimney, and the quote came to €38,000. That is the roof alone. It doesn't touch the damp in the back bedroom, which is a job of its own. The septic tank needs replacing as well, and there is no choice about that one, because the house can't be sold to anybody as it stands. So the €38,000 would only have been the start, and all of it spent on a house with nobody living in it.

I might have talked myself into finding the money all the same. People do, for houses. But there is something else, and I have not told a soul about it until now.

Last February, in the frost, I slipped on the step at the back door. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get myself up. There was nobody to hear me. I did get up in the end, and I told no one, not that evening and not since. You are reading it here before anyone has heard it from my own mouth.

I have been afraid to be at that house by myself ever since. I kept going out, because pipes don't check themselves, but I have not had an easy hour there since that day and I don't expect to have one again. It is not a nice thing to write down at 71, after a working life spent telling small children there was nothing to be frightened of. It is true, though, and I promised myself the hard parts would go in.

So that is the long and the short of it. I can't go on maintaining the house, and I am afraid to be alone at it. Neither of those is going to improve with another winter.

The other half of the why is harder to put into words. It has taken me the best part of two years to come round to it, but I have come round: I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching. Most of you have heard that story more often than you'd wish. I have stood in that haggard many a time since he died, and I can tell you he is not waiting for me in it. Whatever I have of that day, I have it at my own kitchen table as surely as I have it out there, and it will not be signed over to anybody on the 15th of January.

Tom himself would have had no patience with the house being kept as a shrine to him. He always said it should have children in it and not be a museum. Those of you who knew him can hear him saying it. He had good reason to say it, too. He grew up there, and our own children learned to swim in the lake below the house, and the place was never better than when it was full of noise and wet towels. Well, since he died it has been a museum, with one visitor a fortnight, and she only comes to look at the pipes.

I know all of this is easier for me to say than for some of you to hear. For those of you who grew up away, or whose parents did, Glenmore is the place in the photographs and the place the stories come from. I'm not asking you to feel nothing about it. I feel a great deal about it myself. I am only asking you to believe that I thought long and hard before I did this, and that I did not do it lightly or for the money.

That brings me to who is buying it. Their names are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he is no stranger to that side of the country. They have two small children, and they want to live in the house, all the year round, as their home. It is not going to be a holiday let.

You should also know that there was a higher offer. People from Dublin offered more for it in the summer. I took the Joyces' offer, which was lower, and I did it on purpose. The price is a fair one and I am content with it. Pádraig Mulkerrin, Tom's grandfather, built that house in 1931, and it has been a family's house for most of the years since. I wanted the next people through the door to be a family who would be there in February as well as in August, and whose children would get the good of the lake the way ours did. If some of you think I was foolish to leave money behind me, you may tell me so to my face on the 13th of December, which I'll come to shortly.

Now, what is being kept. The dresser is going to Úna's. Pádraig's fiddle is staying in the family, and so are the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the sign from the gate. None of those go with the house. The rest will be cleared before the sale closes. I can't keep everything, and I have stopped trying to.

The Joyces have also said that any of the family can come out and walk the land whenever they like. So the haggard and the lake shore are not shut to us. Anyone home from Boston or Perth or Leeds in the years to come can still go out and stand where their people stood.

Declan, I know you read these, so this part is for you, and I don't mind who else reads it.

You heard about the sale from Gráinne, on WhatsApp. That is no fault of Gráinne's. You should have heard it from me, and before anyone else did. You rang me at two in the morning your time, and you said I was selling Dad. I said things back to you that I should not have said. I won't repeat them here. I take them back, every one.

You were right to be angry about how you found out. There is as much of you in that place as there is of anyone. You are the child who would not come out of the lake until his lips were blue, and no amount of calling from the shore made any difference. I should have talked to you before I agreed to anything. I didn't, and I regret it.

What I will not do is wait until you are home in the summer. I have thought about it, and I can see why it would seem the decent thing to do. But it would mean another winter and another spring of that drive and that back step, and I am not willing to do it. I would rather tell you that straight than let you think it might still be undone.

I am not selling your father. I have set out above, as well as I'm able, what I think I am doing. You may read it and still disagree with me, and if you do, I would much rather hear it from you than not hear from you at all.

I am not angry with you. The door is open and the phone is on, at two in the morning or any other hour.

Now for the invitation, which is for everybody. Before the house is cleared, I want us to have a day in it together. It will be Sunday the 13th of December, and anyone who can come is welcome. There will be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the ground will be soft and I'd like us to walk the land, rain or no rain. We can go through the rooms, go down to the lake, and stand in the haggard where I was proposed to, and those of you who want to tell me I've made a mistake can do it over a bowl of soup. Bring the children. Let me know you're coming so I'll know how much to make, and we can sort out times and lifts between us.

I know well that a Sunday in December, at a few weeks' notice, is no use to most of you overseas, and I'm sorry for that. If you can't be there, the Joyces' offer stands for whenever you are next home, and I will go out with you myself if you want the company.

If you have questions about any of this, ask me. I'd rather answer the same question ten times than have anybody wondering, or hearing a version of it from somebody else.

One last time, so that nobody hears it second-hand again: the sale closes on Friday the 15th of January. If anybody asks you, that is the date, and you have it from me.

With love to every one of you.

I left out a start time for the 13th since you didn't give one, so add it to the invitation paragraph if you've settled on it.
